topic: Breath-holding physiology: CO2 urge, dive reflex, spleen, blackout, record
hook: What holding your breath really does
caption:
The panic you feel when you hold your breath isn't your body running out of oxygen. It's carbon dioxide piling up in your blood and setting off the alarm.

Meanwhile your heart slows and your spleen squeezes out extra red blood cells, the same tricks seals use on deep dives. Facts from Guinness World Records and diving physiology research.

Time yourself right now: how many seconds did you last? Drop it below 👇

carousel_caption:
The panic you feel when you hold your breath isn't your body running out of oxygen. It's carbon dioxide piling up in your blood and setting off the alarm.

Meanwhile your heart slows and your spleen squeezes out extra red blood cells, the same tricks seals use on deep dives. Facts from Guinness World Records and diving physiology research.

Time yourself right now: how many seconds did you last? Drop it below 👇

Cover: What holding your breath really does
📷 Joe Burch (CC BY-SA 3.0) via wikimedia

1/5 It's not about oxygen (CO2)
That burning urge to breathe comes from carbon dioxide building up in your blood, not from running out of oxygen.
📷 Diego Delso (CC BY-SA 4.0) via wikimedia

2/5 Your heart slows down
Put your face in cold water and the dive reflex kicks in, slowing your heartbeat to save oxygen.
🎨 AI-generated image

3/5 Your spleen squeezes
Your spleen contracts and pushes extra red blood cells into your blood. Free divers rely on this boost.
📷 Arek Socha (CC0) via wikimedia

4/5 Your brain overrides you
On land, you would black out first. Then your brainstem restarts your breathing automatically.
📷 unknown (CC BY 4.0) via wikimedia

5/5 The world record (24:37)
In 2021, Budimir Šobat held his breath for 24 min 37 s after breathing pure oxygen first. Don't try it.
📷 jayhem from Antibes, France (CC BY 2.0) via wikimedia
